gravitational-force-s1.title: Scale readings during an elevator ride
gravitational-force-s1.text: A 60 kg student stands on a bathroom scale in an elevator that starts at rest on the ground floor and stops at rest on an upper floor. She records the scale reading at several times. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

gravitational-force-s2.title: Weighing a lander on Mars
gravitational-force-s2.html:
A robotic lander has a mass of 300 kg. Mars has a mass of 6.42 × 10²³ kg and a radius of 3.39 × 10⁶ m. Earth has a mass of 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and a radius of 6.37 × 10⁶ m. Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

The size of the gravitational force between two objects is |Fg| = Gm₁m₂/r², where r is the distance between their centers. The gravitational field at a point is g = Fg/m.

items.q: At 2.0 s the scale reads 660 N. What is the elevator doing then?
options: Speeding up while moving upward
Moving upward at a constant speed
Slowing down while moving upward
At rest, waiting at the ground floor

why.correct: The scale pushes up on the student with 660 N while Earth pulls her down with mg = 588 N. The net force is 72 N up, so she accelerates upward. Starting from rest, that means speeding up on the way up.
options: Right: the normal force exceeds the weight, so the acceleration points up.
At constant speed the scale would read her weight, 588 N.
Slowing down on the way up needs a downward acceleration, so a reading below 588 N.
At rest the scale reads 588 N, her weight.

items.q: What is the size of the elevator's acceleration when the scale reads 660 N, in m/s²?

mistakes.why: Value: that divides the scale reading by the mass. Use the net force, the scale reading minus her weight.

why.correct: Second law for the student, up positive: F_N − mg = ma, so a = (660 N − 588 N) ÷ 60 kg = 72 N ÷ 60 kg = 1.2 m/s² upward.

items.q: At 10.0 s the scale reads 516 N. Which is true at that moment?
options: The gravitational force on her is still 588 N
The gravitational force on her has dropped to 516 N
Her mass has dropped to about 53 kg
The elevator is moving downward at that moment

why.correct: The scale reads the normal force, her apparent weight. The gravitational force mg depends only on her mass and Earth's field, so it stays 588 N; the smaller reading means the acceleration points down (the elevator slows as it nears the top).
options: Right: apparent weight changed, the gravitational force did not.
Earth's pull does not change in an elevator; only the scale's push does.
Her mass does not change during the ride.
A downward acceleration can mean slowing down while moving up, which is what happens near the top floor.

items.q: The cable snaps (safety brakes catch it a moment later). In the instant the elevator and student fall freely together, what does the scale read, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: 588 N is the gravitational force, which still acts. The scale reads the normal force, which is zero when both fall freely together.

why.correct: In free fall both the student and the scale accelerate down at g. Second law for the student: mg − F_N = mg, so F_N = 0. She is weightless: the gravitational force (588 N) still acts, but nothing pushes up on her.

items.q: A student says: "Astronauts in the space station are weightless because there is no gravity up there." Which evidence best contradicts this?
options: Earth's field there is about 90% of its surface value
The astronauts feel no push from the floor
The station is above most of the atmosphere
The astronauts float freely inside the station

why.correct: Gravity at the station's orbit is only about 10% weaker than at the ground; it is what keeps the station in orbit. The astronauts feel weightless because they and the station fall together, so the floor pushes on them with no force: zero apparent weight, like the falling elevator.
options: Right: gravity is nearly as strong; the normal force is what vanishes.
That is the effect, zero normal force, not evidence about whether gravity is present.
The air has nothing to do with gravity's strength.
Floating is what the claim is trying to explain, so it cannot test it.

items.q: What is the strength of the gravitational field at the surface of Mars, in N/kg?

mistakes.why: Value: the radius must be squared. Gravity weakens with the square of the distance.

why.correct: The field is the force per kilogram: g = F_g/m = GM/R² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(6.42 × 10²³) ÷ (3.39 × 10⁶)² = 3.7 N/kg (3.73).

items.q: What is the size of the gravitational force of Mars on the 300 kg lander resting on its surface, in newtons?

mistakes.why: Value: that uses Earth's field. On Mars the field is GM/R² for Mars, about 3.7 N/kg.

why.correct: F_g = mg_Mars = 300 kg × 3.73 N/kg = 1100 N (1.1 × 10³ N). The lander's mass is the same as on Earth; its weight on Mars is about 38% of its weight on Earth.

items.q: The lander leaves Mars and moves to a height above the surface equal to one Mars radius. How does the gravitational force of Mars on it change?
options: It falls to one quarter of its surface value
It falls to one half of its surface value
It stays the same, since the mass is the same
It falls to zero once the lander leaves the surface

why.correct: The distance in Newton's law is measured from the center of Mars: it goes from R to 2R. F ∝ 1/r², so the force becomes 1/2² = 1/4 of its surface value.
options: Right: double the center-to-center distance, a quarter of the force.
The force falls with the square of the distance, not the distance itself.
The masses are the same, but the distance has doubled.
Gravity reaches far beyond a planet's surface; it weakens but does not vanish.

items.q: How does the gravitational force of the lander on Mars compare with the gravitational force of Mars on the lander?
options: They are equal in size
Mars's pull is larger, since Mars is far more massive
The lander exerts no pull on Mars
The lander's pull is larger, since it is closer

why.correct: The two forces are a third-law pair from one interaction, so they are equal in size: Gm₁m₂/r² has both masses in it, the same for each. Mars barely responds because its mass is enormous.
options: Right: the same expression gives both forces.
A larger mass does not let one side of an interaction pull harder.
Every mass attracts every other mass; the pull is two-sided.
Both pulls use the same center-to-center distance.

items.q: Two asteroids attract each other with a force F. If the distance between their centers is tripled, the force becomes
options: 3F

why.correct: F ∝ 1/r²: tripling r divides F by 3² = 9.
options: Right: the square of 3 is 9.
That forgets to square the factor.
Gravity weakens with distance; it does not grow.
Squaring 3 gives 9, not 6.

items.q: Two objects attract with a gravitational force F. If both masses double and the distance between their centers doubles too, the force becomes
options: F
2F
4F

why.correct: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Doubling both masses multiplies the top by 4; doubling r multiplies the bottom by 4. The factors cancel: F.
options: Right: 2 × 2 ÷ 2² = 1.
This counts only one mass doubling.
This forgets the distance in the bottom.
This forgets that both masses doubled.

items.q: A 1000 kg space probe coasts past Earth at a distance of 2 Earth radii from Earth's center (2 × 6.37 × 10⁶ m). Earth's mass is 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg. What is the size of Earth's gravitational force on the probe, in newtons? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg².

mistakes.why: Value: that uses one Earth radius. The probe is 2 radii from Earth's center.
Value: "2 Earth radii from the center" means r = 2R, not a height of 2R above the surface.

why.correct: F = GMm/r² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(5.97 × 10²⁴)(1000) ÷ (1.274 × 10⁷ m)² = 2.5 × 10³ N, a quarter of the 9800 N it would weigh at the surface.

items.q: Near Earth's surface the gravitational field is 9.8 N/kg. What does that number mean?
options: Earth pulls each kilogram with 9.8 N
Each object near Earth weighs 9.8 N
Objects fall at a constant speed of 9.8 m/s
Earth's mass is 9.8 kg per cubic meter

why.correct: The field is the gravitational force per unit mass, g = F/m. A 1 kg object feels 9.8 N; a 5 kg object feels 49 N. It equals the free-fall acceleration, 9.8 m/s², since N/kg = m/s².
options: Right: force per kilogram.
An object's weight depends on its mass: mg.
Free-falling objects speed up by 9.8 m/s each second; their speed is not constant.
The field is a force per mass, not a density.

items.q: A heavy rock and a light pebble are dropped together. The rock has 10 times the mass. With air resistance negligible, which is true?
options: The rock feels 10 times the force; both have the same acceleration
The rock feels 10 times the force and falls 10 times as fast
Both feel the same force and fall with the same acceleration
The rock feels the same force but falls faster since it is heavier

why.correct: Gravitational force is proportional to mass (gravitational mass), and resistance to acceleration is proportional to mass too (inertial mass). a = F/m = (10mg)/(10m) = g. Experiments find these two masses equal, which is why everything falls together.
options: Right: 10 times the force on 10 times the inertia.
Ten times the force acts on ten times the mass, so the acceleration is the same.
The gravitational force is mg, so the rock feels the larger force.
The force on the rock is larger, not equal, and it does not fall faster.

items.q: A student's mass is 55 kg. She stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating downward at 2.0 m/s². What does the scale read, in newtons? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

mistakes.why: Value: that adds the accelerations. With the acceleration down, the scale pushes up less than her weight: F_N = m(g − a).
Value: that is her weight. The scale reads less while she accelerates downward.

why.correct: Down positive: mg − F_N = ma, so F_N = m(g − a) = 55 kg × (9.8 − 2.0) m/s² = 430 N (429 N rounded).

items.q: Order these elevator moments from the largest scale reading to the smallest, for the same rider.
options: Moving down and slowing to a stop
Moving up at a constant speed
Moving up and slowing to a stop
Falling freely after the cable breaks

why.correct: Slowing while moving down is an upward acceleration, so F_N > mg; constant speed gives F_N = mg; slowing while moving up is a downward acceleration, F_N < mg; free fall gives F_N = 0.
